*This method allows calculation of any type of planar cell, skewed or non-skewed*

Till now it has been assumed throughout that all variables vary linearly inside a cell, i.e. the gradient inside a cell is constant. This information can be used to compute the area of a cell. It involves a bit of Vector Algebra and Calculus, but its really amazing. 

# Divergence Theorem 
The gauss divergence theorem states that for any vector field $B$ the following equality holds, 
$$
\int_V (\nabla\cdot\textbf{B})\; dV = \oint_{\partial V} (\textbf{B}\cdot\hat{n})\;dA
$$ 

using depth integration and coordinate transformations, the equation can be rewritten as, 

$$
\int_S (\nabla\cdot\textbf{B})\; dS = \oint_{\partial S} (\textbf{B}\cdot\hat{n})\; dL 
$$ 

> Please refer to [this](/docs/report/10_implementation.html#jacobian-determinants) for why the coordinate transformation determinant (jacobian) was taken to be $1$ 

# Computing Areas 

Now how to calculate the areas? If we somehow find a vector field $B$ such that $\nabla\cdot\textbf{B}=1$ then the equation transforms into 
$$
S_P = \oint_{\partial S} (\textbf{B}\cdot\hat{n})\;dL = \sum_{edges} \int_L(\textbf{B}\cdot\hat{n})\;dL
$$ 

The line integral was expanded to a summation over all edges of a cell. Notice the vector field $B = \frac13 (x,y,z)$ 
$$
\nabla\cdot\textbf{B} = \frac13 (\frac{\partial}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial}{\partial z})\cdot(x,y,z) = \frac13 (1+1+1) = 1
$$

Using this vector field, the area of the cell can be approximated as 
$$
S_P = \sum_{edges} \int_L(\textbf{B}\cdot\hat{n})\;dL \approx \sum_{edges} (\textbf{B}_e\cdot\hat{n_e})\;L_e = \sum_{edges} (\frac13 (x_e, y_e, z_e) \cdot \hat{n_e})\;L_e 
$$

where $(x_e,y_e,z_e)$ is with respect to the cell center. This is a reliable way to find the area of any cell in general, skewed or non-skewed and is not too computationally expensive. 

The running time complexity of this algorithm for computing the areas of all cells is $\mathcal{O}(E)$ where $E$ is the total number of edges of mesh.
